A patch that causes a device to fail staging checks is held back until the root cause is identified and a remediation plan is recorded.

Staging test outcomes are recorded in the change record. A failed staging test does not automatically block production deployment; the Head of Infrastructure assesses risk and may authorise a targeted rollout with enhanced monitoring.

## 7 Exceptions

Exceptions to this policy — for example, an equipment vendor that no longer provides patches, or a legacy device for which no staged test environment exists — require written approval from the Head of Infrastructure.

An exception is tracked in ITSM and expires after 90 days. The owner of the exception must request a renewal before expiry. Unrenewed exceptions are escalated to the Service Delivery Manager.

The Head of Infrastructure reviews all open exceptions quarterly as part of the baseline review described in Section 2.

title: Incident Management Process
body:
# Incident Management Process

## 1. Purpose

This process governs incident management at Norvane Managed IT Services Oy,
covering roles, timelines, and communication requirements for every severity
level. Severity definitions follow DOC-006.

## 2. Ticket lifecycle

Every incident progresses through these stages:

1. **New**
2. **Triaged**
3. **Assigned**
4. **In progress**
5. **Resolved**
6. **Closed**

Re-opening is permitted within five business days of closure without manual
approval. A resolved ticket not re-opened is auto-closed after 10 business days.

## 3. Triage

Triage must be completed within 15 minutes of ticket creation during business
hours (07:00–18:00 EET/EEST, Monday to Friday, excluding Finnish public
holidays). During out-of-hours periods the target is the next page interval of
the on-call rota.

The triaging engineer must confirm or assign a severity (P1–P4) per DOC-006,
assign a responsible engineer from the appropriate rota or team, record the
customer tier and the applicable response window, and add a triage note
describing observed symptoms and initial diagnostic steps.

## 4. Escalation

The escalation rules are:

- A P1 is escalated to the duty manager within 30 minutes of ticket creation,
  regardless of current status.
- A P2 that is unassigned after 30 minutes is escalated to the duty manager.
- A P1 that reaches 50% of its resolution window without a confirmed fix is
  escalated to the Head of Infrastructure.

The Service Delivery Manager must be informed of any P1 that breaches the SLA
response or resolution window.

## 5. Major incident management

A major incident is declared when a P1 affects more than one customer or has
lasted for more than two hours without resolution. Upon declaration:

- An incident commander is named within 10 minutes. The incident commander is
  separate from the duty engineer and coordinates the response.
- A dedicated major-incident bridge call or chat channel is opened immediately.
- Status updates are issued every 30 minutes to all affected customers and to
  the Service Delivery Manager. Updates must include the current status, the
  estimated time to the next update, and any customer-facing actions required.
- All subsequent changes during the major incident are logged under a single
  change ticket referencing the incident ID.

## 6. Customer communication

Platinum and Gold customers receive telephone notification from the duty engineer
within the response window defined in DOC-006, followed by a formal email
summary within one hour.

Silver and Bronze customers receive an email notification within the response
window. Telephone notification is not automatic but may be initiated by the
incident commander for P1 events.

## 7. Postmortems

A written postmortem is required for every P1 incident within 10 business days
of resolution. Postmortems for P2 incidents are optional and at the duty
manager's discretion.

Postmortems are conducted under a blameless framework. Every postmortem must
include a summary and timeline, impact assessment, root cause, detection and
response assessment, contributing factors, a description of what went well,
action items with named owners and due dates, and lessons learned. Open action
items must be published in the team backlog; closed items must include their
completion dates.

Postmortems are stored in the Service Desk repository. A customer-facing
summary is extracted per section 6.

## 8. Closure and records

An incident is closed when the service is restored or a workaround is in place,
all required communications have been sent, and the postmortem (if required) has
been completed and filed.

Closed incidents are retained in the ITSM system for a minimum of three years.

title: Change Management Policy
body:
# Change Management Policy

## 1 Purpose

This policy establishes the framework under which all changes to Norvane's
production infrastructure, managed services, and supporting systems are planned
and recorded. The objective is to reduce unplanned service disruption while
maintaining sufficient agility.

## 2 Scope

This policy applies to every person employed by Norvane or engaged as a
subcontractor who creates, modifies, or removes configuration items in a
production environment. It covers all infrastructure documented in the network
architecture overview (DOC-010), including DC1 (Helsinki Pasila), DC2 (Tampere
Kaleva), and all managed customer sites.

Specific processes under this policy include the firewall rule-change process
in DOC-013 and the patching windows in DOC-022. Incidents arising from changes
are handled according to DOC-023.

## 3 Change categories

Changes fall into three categories:

**Standard changes** are pre-approved, low-risk, and repeatable. They follow a
documented procedure and carry no risk of service disruption. Examples include
routine firewall rule additions within an approved range, password resets for
managed accounts, and adding a single access-port assignment to an existing
VLAN. Standard changes do not require CAB review.

**Normal changes** are any change that does not qualify as standard. Each must
be raised as a Change Request (CR) with a change ID in the format CHG-YYYY-NNNN.
It is assessed by the CAB before implementation. Typical lead time is five
business days.

**Emergency changes** are changes that must be implemented immediately to
restore service, address a security vulnerability, or comply with a statutory
requirement. The emergency process is governed by DOC-013 when the change
involves a firewall rule. Emergency changes are approved by the Head of
Infrastructure (or the Security Lead for security-specific changes) and receive
retrospective CAB review within five business days.

## 4 The CAB

The Change Advisory Board meets weekly, normally on Tuesdays at 10:00 EET.
Quorum is three members. The CAB is chaired by the Head of Infrastructure and
its membership is fixed:

- The Head of Infrastructure (chair)
- The Security Lead
- The Service Delivery Manager
- A Service Desk representative

Decisions are recorded on the change ticket. The CAB may convene ad hoc when
an urgent matter requires assessment outside the scheduled meeting.

## 5 Risk assessment and backout

Every normal change and every emergency change requires a written risk
assessment and a backout plan. The risk assessment covers the expected impact,
the affected services, and the execution window.

The backout plan names the trigger condition under which the change is reversed
and identifies the person authorised to invoke it. That person must not be the
sole implementer; at least one second person must confirm that backout conditions
have been met. The backout plan is reviewed and acknowledged by the CAB before
a normal change is approved.

## 6 Change freeze

Change freeze periods during which only emergency changes are permitted are:

- 23 December to 2 January inclusive (annual holiday freeze)
- Any period a Customer has defined in their contract as a peak trading period

During a freeze, normal and standard changes are suspended. Emergency changes
require written approval of the Head of Infrastructure and are recorded with
the reason code `FREEZE_OVERRIDE`.

## 7 Failed changes

A failed change is one that produces an unintended outcome requiring backout,
service degradation, or a corrective change after CAB approval. Every failed
change is reviewed at the next CAB meeting with a written post-implementation
review (PIR).

Three failed changes of the same type in a single quarter trigger an automatic
design review by the Security Lead and the Head of Infrastructure. The design
review examines the underlying architecture or procedure that repeatedly fails
and recommends corrective action before further changes of that type are
approved.

## 8 Records

All changes are recorded in the ITSM system with their assigned CHG-YYYY-NNNN
identifier. CAB meeting minutes, the approved change schedule, PIR reports, and design-review output are documented for at least two years.

title: Data Classification and Handling Policy
body:
# Data Classification and Handling Policy

## 1 Purpose

This policy establishes the classification levels used by Norvane and the
handling requirements for information Norvane creates, processes, stores, or
transmits on behalf of its Customers. It ensures data
receives protection commensurate with its sensitivity and helps Norvane meet
obligations under Customer contracts and applicable data-protection regulations.

## 2 Scope

This policy applies to every Norvane employee, contractor, and subcontractor
who handles Customer data or Norvane internal data. It covers all media —
electronic, paper, and cloud-stored — and all environments: on-premise systems
at DC1 and DC2, remote workstations, customer sites, and third-party platforms where Norvane stores or processes data.

DOC-041 governs how privileged access to classified information is provisioned
and audited. Customer-facing data obligations under DOC-002 are set out in the
relevant contracts and service descriptions; this policy defines the internal
requirements Norvane follows to meet them.

## 3 Classification levels

Norvane uses four classification levels:

**Public** — Information Norvane is authorised to make available to anyone.
Examples: marketing material published on the Norvane website, published
service catalogues, and press releases.

**Internal** — Information for use within Norvane and, where contractually
permitted, the Customer's operational teams. Examples: internal policies,
runbooks, network diagrams, and internal reports.

**Confidential** — Information whose unauthorised disclosure could cause
commercial harm, regulatory exposure, or reputational damage. Examples: customer
contracts, incident records, asset inventories, and financial data.

**Restricted** — The highest tier. Information whose compromise could result in
serious harm to individuals, statutory breach, or significant contractual
penalty. Examples: health and patient data, legal client files, credentials and
encryption keys, authentication logs, and data classified as special category
under the EU General Data Protection Regulation.

## 4 Handling requirements

The table below specifies minimum handling requirements for each level:

| Requirement | Public | Internal | Confidential | Restricted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Storage** | Any authorised system | Encrypted at rest | Encrypted at rest | Encrypted at rest and in transit |
| **Transmission** | Unencrypted permitted | TLS or equivalent | TLS 1.2 minimum | End-to-end encryption |
| **Access** | No restriction | Role-based; documented justification | Least-privilege; documented justification | Named-individual; approved by Security Lead and the Customer; access logging reviewed monthly |
| **Retention** | Until obsolete | Minimum two years | Contractual plus two years | Contractual minimum; extended for health data |
| **Destruction** | Standard deletion | Secure deletion (overwrite or degauss) | Cryptographic erasure or certified destruction | Certifiable destruction with witnessed certification |

## 5 Marking and sharing

Every document, file, or data extract produced or held by Norvane carries a
classification label, visible in the document frontmatter and, where feasible,
in the file metadata. Sharing classified data outside Norvane requires the
owner's written approval.

## 6 Third-party and cross-border transfer

Confidential or Restricted data must not be transferred outside the EEA or to
a country without an adequacy decision from the European Commission unless the
Customer has given explicit written approval. When approval is given, Norvane
records it on the relevant service record and notifies the Security Lead.
Third-party vendors processing such data must be subject to a data-processing
agreement incorporating equivalent classification requirements.

## 7 Breach reporting

A suspected data breach must be reported to the Security Lead within 24 hours. The Security Lead assesses the event and, where confirmed, coordinates notification to the supervisory authority and to any affected Customer within 72 hours. Customer notification describes the nature
of the breach, the categories and volume of data affected, and the measures
taken. This policy references GDPR and Finnish health-data obligations without quoting legislation.

## 8 Review

This policy is reviewed at least annually or when triggered by a change in
applicable legislation, a material breach, or a Customer contract amendment.
The Security Lead proposes updates; the Service Delivery Manager reviews
operational impact. Approved changes are communicated to staff and published on SharePoint within five business days.

title: Postmortem PM-2025-17 — Core Switch Failure at Cobalt
body:
# Postmortem PM-2025-17 — Core Switch Failure at Cobalt

**Incident:** INC-2025-0311 · **Customer:** Cobalt Retail Group (Gold, CUST-03) · **Date:** 2025-09-12 · **Severity:** P1 · **Status:** closed

## Summary

At 03:20 EET on 2025-09-12 the Cobalt Retail Group (Gold, CUST-03) headquarters site lost all IP connectivity, taking down POS traffic for all five retail stores. The outage lasted 252 minutes (03:20 → 07:32) and was classified as a P1. The root cause was a failed power supply unit on switch `sw-core-c1` (Catalyst 9500-24Y4C) combined with a configuration error: the stack's power redundancy mode was `combined` rather than `redundant`, so a single PSU failure triggered a full stack reboot. A service credit of EUR 18,400 was issued.

## Timeline

- **03:20** — Zabbix P1 alert: all stack members and connected sites down.
- **03:27** — On-call engineer acknowledged. P1 ticket created.
- **03:41** — First customer contacts; store POS terminals reported dark.
- **04:15** — Investigation redirected to suspected fibre failure. A 40-minute dead end: patch panels and optical power tested, fibre confirmed healthy. The core switch was not inspected.
- **05:05** — On-site engineer dispatched to Cobalt HQ. Observed Catalyst 9500 cycling through `reload` messages at least four times.
- **05:50** — Suspect PSU replaced in `sw-core-c1`. The switch entered another reload cycle within three minutes.
- **06:30** — Shared console session identified the `combined` power redundancy mode. Changed to `redundant`, issued a clean reload.
- **07:32** — Services verified. Incident resolved.

## Impact

All five Cobalt Retail stores lost POS and intranet connectivity for 252 minutes. No data loss was reported. The Gold-tier SLA breach required a EUR 18,400 service credit against the 20 % maximum.

## Root cause

Two co-factors caused the outage:

1. **Hardware failure.** PSU-2 on `sw-core-c1` failed during a planned building electrical maintenance window at Cobalt HQ. The facilities team advised of a load transfer but raised no specific alert about the switch PSU.

2. **Configuration error.** The Catalyst 9500 stack power redundancy mode was `combined` instead of `redundant`. In `combined` mode a single-unit failure triggers a full stack reboot; in `redundant` mode the spare PSU absorbs the failure. The correct mode was documented in DOC-012, but an earlier stack expansion had overwritten the setting and the deviation was never caught by a configuration audit.

## Detection

Zabbix detected the outage within its 60-second polling interval, picking up loss of reachability on all `cobalt-hq` interfaces and store VPN endpoints. The alert was automatically elevated to P1.

## Response

The on-call engineer followed the P1 escalation path in DOC-023. The initial diagnosis misidentified the cause as a fibre failure — a 40-minute detour that extended the outage but is documented transparently. Once the on-site engineer identified the repeated reload pattern, the investigation pivoted to the switch hardware. The root cause was remediated at 06:30.

## Contributing factors

- The `combined` power redundancy mode on `sw-core-c1` deviated from DOC-012 and was not caught by configuration audits.
- Cobalt's entire store network depended on a single stack at headquarters; a second stack would have contained the blast radius.
- The building's electrical maintenance was communicated only by email (DOC-022) but not flagged for monitoring.
- The NOC runbook lacks a "repeated stack reload" diagnostic branch, delaying the correct diagnosis after the fibre dead-end was cleared.

## What went well

- Zabbix detected the outage within the polling interval and the alert was correctly elevated to P1.
- The on-call engineer acknowledged within seven minutes — well within the 30-minute P1 target for Gold.
- An on-site engineer was dispatched within one hour.

## Action items

| # | Action | Owner | Due | Status |
|---|--------|-------|-----|--------|
| 1 | Audit power redundancy mode on all Catalyst 9500 and 9300 stacks. Correct any running in `combined`. | Marko Heinänen | 2025-10-10 | **Completed** — three stacks corrected at CUST-03 and CUST-01. |
| 2 | Add a mandatory section on power redundancy configuration to DOC-012, prohibiting `combined` mode. | Marko Heinänen | 2025-12-08 | **Completed** — landed in DOC-012 v2.4. |
| 3 | Add a Zabbix alert for repeated stack reloads (three or more reboots per hour) on core and distribution switches. | Marko Heinänen | 2026-01-31 | **STILL OPEN** |
| 4 | Update the NOC runbook to include the "repeated stack reload" diagnostic path. | Tuomas Virta | 2025-11-30 | **STILL OPEN** |

## Lessons learned

Hardware redundancy configured in the hardware but not in the configuration is not redundancy. The Cobalt Catalyst 9500 had two PSU units physically present, but the `combined` mode meant a single failure took the entire stack offline. Configuration audits that check interfaces and routing protocols but not operational modes like power redundancy will miss this gap. The audit in Action Item 1 should be repeated every six months as a runbook procedure, not left to a one-off exercise.

title: Postmortem PM-2026-03 — DNS Misconfiguration at Brambleby
body:
# Postmortem PM-2026-03 — DNS Misconfiguration at Brambleby

**Incident:** INC-2026-0052 · **Customer:** Brambleby Logistics Ltd (Silver, CUST-02) · **Date:** 2026-02-08 · **Severity:** P2 · **Status:** closed

## Summary

On 2026-02-08 between 07:40 and 09:45 EET, Brambleby Logistics Ltd (Silver, CUST-02) lost name resolution at both sites in Turku. IP connectivity was unaffected. Applications dependent on DNS — the ERP system, internal web portal, and file shares — were inaccessible. The incident was classified as a P2 (125 minutes). No downtime was recorded because only name resolution was affected. The P2 response SLA was breached. No service credit was issued because the duration did not reach Brambleby's credit floor. The root cause was a DHCP scope option 006 change the previous evening that replaced the configured pair of DNS server addresses with a single address. When that resolver was patched at 07:30, clients had no name resolution.

## Timeline

- **2026-02-07 21:10** — A network engineer applied a DHCP scope option 006 change to the Brambleby scope. The configuration tool accepted only a single address; the engineer entered the primary resolver, replacing the ordered pair. No notification was sent to the Service Desk or customers.
- **07:40** — First user report: ERP system would not open. Service Desk created ticket INC-2026-0052.
- **08:05** — Ticket triaged as P2. IP connectivity tests successful; issue isolated to DNS resolution.
- **08:20** — On-call engineer compared the active DHCP scope against the documented standard and identified that option 006 contained a single address instead of the expected pair.
- **08:55** — The correct ordered pair was restored. Change applied live.
- **09:45** — Post-change verification confirmed clients had renewed with correct DNS entries. Incident resolved.

## Impact

The ERP system, internal web portal, and file shares were inaccessible because these services rely on DNS name resolution. IP connectivity was unaffected throughout. The outage was classified as degraded service because the underlying network infrastructure remained fully functional — name resolution was the sole affected component. No data loss occurred.

## Root cause

A DHCP scope option 006 change on the evening of 2026-02-07 replaced the configured ordered pair of DNS server addresses with a single address. The configuration tool accepted only a single value; the engineer entered the primary resolver, and the secondary was not included. When clients renewed their DHCP leases on 2026-02-08 morning, they received a scope with only one DNS server.

At approximately 07:30, that single DNS resolver was patched as part of a separate maintenance activity — a routine firmware update that took the resolver offline. With no secondary DNS server on the scope, Brambleby clients had no name resolution available.

The change was categorised as a standard change, which permits implementation without a post-change verification test. Had a name resolution test been performed after the change, the misconfiguration would have been detected before users were affected.

## Detection

No automated monitoring detected the outage. Zabbix monitors reachability through HTTP and ICMP probes, but these use cached DNS entries or direct IP targets and did not fail. No synthetic DNS query probe was configured for the Brambleby site. The incident was first detected through user reports at 07:40.

## Response

The Service Desk created and triaged the incident as P2 at 08:05. The on-call engineer identified the misconfiguration at 08:20 by comparing the live scope against the documented standard — a manual process that relied on checking scope options against the DNS and DHCP standards document. The remediation was applied at 08:55, and a post-change verification queried live clients for their DNS assignment. The incident was communicated to the Brambleby account manager via email at 08:15 and 09:45.

## Contributing factors

- The change was made under the standard change category, which does not require a CAB review or a mandatory post-change test. Changes altering client-facing network settings, including DHCP scope options defining core network parameters, should have been elevated to a normal change requiring CAB review per DOC-024.
- No post-change verification covered name resolution. The change checklist includes connectivity testing but does not specify a DNS resolution test for DHCP changes.

## What went well

- The Service Desk correctly classified the incident as P2 and did not investigate a P1.
- The on-call engineer identified the root cause within 40 minutes by comparing the live scope against the documented standard.

## Action items

| # | Action | Owner | Due | Status |
|---|--------|-------|-----|--------|
| 1 | Reclassify DHCP scope option changes as normal changes requiring CAB review per DOC-024. | Marko Heinänen | 2026-03-31 | **Completed** — updated 2026-03-16. |
| 2 | Add a name-resolution check to the post-change verification steps in the change implementation checklist. | Tuomas Virta | 2026-04-30 | **STILL OPEN** |
| 3 | Assign an owner and review date to the DNS and DHCP standards document. | Marko Heinänen | 2026-03-31 | **STILL OPEN** |

## Lessons learned

A DHCP scope is not a configuration setting; it is a runtime contract for every client that leases from it. Changes affecting name resolution have the same impact as changing DNS servers and should be treated with equal rigour. The DNS and DHCP standards document is the authoritative source, but when a document has no named owner and no review cycle, it cannot function as a living standard. An unowned document is a single point of failure. Action Item 3 addresses this structural weakness.

title: Postmortem PM-2026-07 — Failed Backup Restore at Aurora
body:
# Postmortem PM-2026-07 — Failed Backup Restore at Aurora

**Incident:** INC-2026-0095 · **Customer:** Aurora Health District (Platinum, CUST-01) · **Date:** 2026-04-21 · **Severity:** P1 · **Status:** closed

## Summary

On 2026-04-21 the file-services volume for aurora-hq was corrupted at 01:15 EET by a failed storage controller firmware update. Aurora Health District (CUST-01, Platinum tier) experienced a P1 outage lasting 665 minutes until 12:20 when services were verified. Norvane invoked the documented restore procedure defined in DOC-018. Two systemic failures emerged during recovery.

First, the most recent recoverable copy on bkparr-01 was 9 hours old. The nightly backup job had been failing silently since 2026-04-20 16:00, and replication to bkparr-02 carried the same stale point because both appliances follow the same schedule (DOC-018 section 3). The 1-hour RPO was missed by 8 hours, and the last 9 hours of clinical correspondence files were unrecoverable from backup.

Second, the whole-volume restore took 11 hours 05 minutes against a 4-hour RTO target. The restore ran at SAN disk speed rather than the expected file-level or application-level restore, resulting in a prolonged data-unavailability window for the Aurora Health District staff.

The customer credit of EUR 24,000 was applied per DOC-002.

## Timeline

| Time (EET) | Event |
|---|---|
| 01:15 | Storage controller firmware update fails; aurora-hq file-services volume is corrupted |
| 01:40 | Restore decision made; Backup & Storage Engineer begins recovery |
| 02:30 | Restore initiated from the most recent image on bkparr-01 |
| 04:00 | First indication that the restore point is 9 hours old (the nightly job failure from 2026-04-20 16:00) |
| 06:00 | Duty manager escalates to Service Delivery Manager |
| 09:15 | Customer informed of the data-loss window (01:15 → 10:15 on 2026-04-20) |
| 11:30 | Volume comes online after 11 hours 05 minutes of restore |
| 12:20 | Services verified as operational; incident resolved |

## Impact

- aurora-hq file-services volume offline for 665 minutes (01:15 → 12:20 EET).
- Platinum availability target of 99.95% breached.
- 1-hour RPO target missed by 8 hours; 9 hours of clinical correspondence data unrecoverable.
- 4-hour RTO target exceeded; actual restore time was 11 hours 05 minutes.
- Service credit of EUR 24,000 issued to the customer.

## Root cause

The primary root cause is a process failure. A failed storage controller firmware update corrupted the aurora-hq file-services volume at 01:15. Norvane executed the correct documented procedure from DOC-018. However, two downstream conditions degraded the outcome:

1. **Silent backup job failure.** The nightly backup job on bkparr-01 had been failing since 2026-04-20 16:00. Replication to bkparr-02 carried the same stale data because it mirrors the source schedule and only begins after the source job completes successfully (DOC-018 section 3). The failure was not surfaced to the on-call rota because the alert trigger watched the appliance job status rather than the protected-object status.

2. **Restored volume took 11 hours 05 minutes.** The whole-volume restore at SAN disk speed far exceeded the documented estimate of approximately 2 hours (DOC-018 section 5). The restore was running from the correct procedure; the discrepancy was between the documented performance expectations and the actual I/O throughput of the bkparr-01 → aurora-hq path.

## Detection

The corruption was detected at 01:15 through the Zabbix monitoring platform, which polls at 60-second intervals and processes SNMP traps immediately (DOC-021 section 3). A P1 ticket was opened. The backup job failure itself was not surfaced at the time because the Platinum immediate alert is configured to watch the appliance job status, not the protected-object status.

## Response

1. The Backup & Storage Engineer assessed the corruption and confirmed a restore was necessary.
2. The restore was initiated from the most recent image on bkparr-01 per DOC-018 section 5.
3. At 04:00, the engineer identified that the restore point was 9 hours stale and flagged the issue.
4. The duty manager was escalated to at 06:00. The Service Delivery Manager was notified at 09:15 with the data-loss window.
5. The restore completed at 11:30; services were verified operational by 12:20.

## Contributing factors

1. **Alert on job status, not protected objects.** The alert configuration monitors the appliance job status rather than the state of the protected objects themselves. If the alert watched the protected-object status, the backup failure would have been surfaced to the on-call rota within minutes of the first failure at 2026-04-20 16:00, not the following morning. This applies across all tiers; Silver and Bronze failures are aggregated into the morning review per DOC-021 section 3, but the Platinum alert did not fire at all.

2. **Backup replication carries stale data.** The replication schedule on bkparr-02 mirrors bkparr-01 and does not start until the source job succeeds. When the source fails silently, both appliances hold the same outdated data. This was noted as a gap in DOC-018 section 7.

3. **Restore performance discrepancy.** The runbook estimates approximately 2 hours for a whole-volume restore (DOC-018 section 5). The actual restore took 11 hours 05 minutes. No performance benchmarking against the aurora-hq → bkparr-01 restore path has been conducted to validate the documented estimate.

4. **Disaster recovery plan validation is not supported by operational evidence.** DOC-019 section 8 records that a full disaster recovery test was carried out on 2024-11-16 in which all tiers were exercised and all objectives were met. The operational record shows that this test covered only the file-services tier and did not perform a restore of the clinical database tier. The clinical database tier had never been restored end to end in the Norvane environment; restore tests were conducted at vendor level only. The claim in DOC-019 section 8 that restore testing is "performed twice yearly across all backup tiers" is therefore not supported by operational evidence. DOC-018 section 6 states that restore tests "cover the file-services tier only" and that "database restores are tested at vendor level, not end to end in the Norvane environment." The validation section of DOC-019 has not been revised to reflect what is actually tested.

5. **Replication lag is not alerted on.** Replication lag between bkparr-01 and bkparr-02 is collected and displayed on the dashboard but generates no alert (DOC-021 section 6). A significant lag would have been visible on the dashboard but was not surfaced to on-call staff.

## What went well

- The P1 was activated immediately when the storage controller failure was detected, triggering the on-call rota without delay.
- The correct runbook (DOC-018) was followed throughout the restore operation.
- The Service Desk team maintained regular communication with the customer, including notification of the data-loss window at 09:15.
- The restore was completed within a reasonable timeframe given the constraints of working with a stale backup point.

## Action items

| # | Action | Owner | Due date | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Configure alerts on protected-object failures rather than appliance job status | Marko Heinänen | 2026-06-30 | Completed 2026-06-11 |
| 2 | Configure alerts on replication lag between bkparr-01 and bkparr-02 | Emil Nyberg | 2026-06-30 | Still open |
| 3 | Schedule an end-to-end restore test of the clinical database tier | Emil Nyberg | 2026-09-30 | Still open |
| 4 | Revise the validation section of DOC-019 to reflect what is actually tested | Marko Heinänen | 2026-06-30 | Still open |

## Lessons learned

1. **Alert on protected-object status, not job status.** Monitoring the appliance's job status alone is insufficient to detect backup failures. When the protected object is the thing that matters, the alert must watch the protected object.

2. **Replication lag must be alerted on.** The dashboard display is not sufficient; active alerting is required. As documented in DOC-021 section 6, replication lag is not alerted on. This is a gap that must be closed.

3. **Disaster recovery plan validation must reflect reality.** A DR test report claiming all tiers were exercised must be supported by evidence. When the operational record shows that only the file-services tier has been restored end to end, the plan must be updated to reflect that. Testing must cover every tier that the plan claims to cover.

title: Postmortem PM-2026-11 — Upstream Fibre Outage at Eastgate
body:
# Postmortem PM-2026-11 — Upstream Fibre Outage at Eastgate

**Incident:** INC-2026-0128 · **Customer:** Eastgate Housing Association (Bronze, CUST-06) · **Date:** 2026-06-29 · **Severity:** P1 · **Status:** closed

## Summary

On 2026-06-29 the upstream connectivity for Eastgate Housing Association (CUST-06, Bronze tier) was disrupted when a third-party contractor cutting a duct during street works damaged the Vantage Fibre primary circuit VF-HEL-4471. The backup circuit VF-HEL-4472 did not fail over because both circuits share the last 400 metres of duct into the building, and the same duct was cut. Eastgate's two sites (eastgate-offices and eastgate-sheltered-housing) were offline for 6 hours 40 minutes (05:05 → 11:45 EEST). No telecare calls were lost; the sheltered-housing telecare system runs on a separate GSM path that was unaffected by the street works.

The incident was classified as P1. The Bronze availability target of 99.00% was missed. A service credit of EUR 3,100 was issued to the customer, capped at the 5% Bronze limit per DOC-002. A vendor credit of EUR 1,850 was claimed from Vantage Fibre within the 30-day contractual window.

## Timeline

| Time (EEST) | Event |
|---|---|
| 05:05 | Zabbix monitoring detects upstream circuit down; alert fired |
| 05:12 | On-call engineer acknowledges the alert |
| 05:30 | Ticket raised with Vantage Fibre NOC as Critical |
| 06:10 | Vantage Fibre confirms street-works cable strike as the cause |
| 07:00 | Norvane establishes that the backup circuit VF-HEL-4472 is also down; shared-duct issue raised internally |
| 09:20 | Vantage Fibre splice team arrives on site |
| 11:20 | Primary circuit restored by Vantage Fibre |
| 11:45 | Eastgate services verified as operational; incident resolved |

## Impact

- Both Eastgate sites (eastgate-offices and eastgate-sheltered-housing) offline for 6 hours 40 minutes.
- Bronze availability target of 99.00% breached.
- Service credit of EUR 3,100 issued to the customer (capped at 5% of monthly fee, the Bronze limit per DOC-002).
- No sheltered-housing telecare calls lost (telecare runs on a separate GSM path).
- Vendor credit of EUR 1,850 claimed from Vantage Fib Oy within the 30-day window.

## Root cause

The root cause category is upstream_provider. A third-party contractor, executing approved street works, cut through a fibre duct containing the Vantage Fibre primary circuit VF-HEL-4471. The circuit went down immediately.

Norvane's upstream architecture provides two circuits: VF-HEL-4471 (1 Gbit/s symmetric primary) and VF-HEL-4472 (300/100 Mbit/s backup). The edge firewalls control failover between them. The backup circuit VF-HEL-4472 did not take over because both circuits share the last 400 metres of duct into the building. The street works cut through that shared duct section, taking both circuits down simultaneously.

The procurement record for the backup circuit, held in DOC-007, notes the shared duct in 2023. This note was never acted upon. Norvane's network architecture documentation (DOC-010) describes the two paths as "geographically diverse fibre paths with no shared physical infrastructure" (DOC-010 section 5). This description does not match the actual physical reality.

## Detection

Zabbix detected the circuit failure at 05:05 via its 60-second polling and BGP-peer-down alert rule, which fires immediately (DOC-021 section 3, "BGP or upstream peer down — P1 — Immediate"). The alert was acknowledged within 7 minutes. The detection of the primary circuit failure was timely; the detection that the backup circuit was also down took longer because the initial assumption was that the backup path would have already taken over.

## Response

1. The on-call engineer acknowledged the alert at 05:12 and opened the incident ticket.
2. At 05:30, the Vantage Fibre NOC was contacted and the issue was raised as Critical.
3. At 06:10, the vendor confirmed the cause as a street-works cable strike.
4. At 07:00, the engineer verified that the backup circuit VF-HEL-4472 was also down and raised the shared-duct issue internally with the Head of Infrastructure.
5. The Service Delivery Manager notified the customer of the outage and the upstream nature of the cause.
6. The vendor splice team was on site at 09:20 and restored the circuit at 11:20.
7. Services were verified at 11:45 and the incident was closed.

## Contributing factors

1. **Shared duct between primary and backup circuits.** VF-HEL-4471 and VF-HEL-4472 share the last 400 metres of duct into the DC1 building. A cut in that duct takes both circuits down, eliminating the diversity that the backup circuit is intended to provide. This was recorded in the procurement documentation for the backup circuit in 2023 (DOC-007) but was never remediated.

2. **Architecture documentation does not match physical reality.** DOC-010 section 5 states that "DC1 and DC2 sit on geographically diverse fibre paths with no shared physical infrastructure" and that the two sites are connected "over separate right-of-way routes, eliminating any single-point-of-failure risk in the transport layer between them." For the upstream circuits at DC1, the two paths are not independent in the final segment. The procurement record in DOC-007 captures the shared-duct detail that the architecture document omits.

3. **Procurement note not acted upon.** The procurement record for VF-HEL-4472 noted the shared duct in 2023. No action was taken to remedy the issue, commission a separate path, or at minimum flag the risk in the customer's site plan. This is a process gap: identified risk was recorded but never escalated to resolution.

4. **No pre-armed failover test.** The backup circuit failover was not tested prior to the outage. A quarterly failover test would have revealed the shared-duct dependency before a real incident exposed it. The quarterly service review for Eastgate does not include a failover test.

## What went well

- Zabbix detected the outage within seconds; the alert fired immediately per the monitoring thresholds in DOC-021.
- The on-call engineer acknowledged the alert within 7 minutes and raised the vendor NOC ticket promptly.
- The vendor met its 30-minute response SLA; the splice team was dispatched and arrived on site within 4 hours 15 minutes of the initial report.
- The vendor credit of EUR 1,850 was claimed within the 30-day contractual window.
- Telecare services were unaffected; the GSM path for sheltered-housing telecare is independent of the fibre circuits and functioned throughout the incident.

## Action items

| # | Action | Owner | Due date | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Commission a genuinely diverse second path for DC1 (separate duct, separate right-of-way) | Marko Heinänen | 2027-03-31 | Still open |
| 2 | Correct the resilience section of DOC-010 to reflect the shared-duct reality | Marko Heinänen | 2026-08-31 | Still open |
| 3 | Review all customer sites for single-homed or shared-duct upstream circuits | Marko Heinänen | 2026-09-30 | Still open |
| 4 | Add a pre-armed failover test of the upstream circuits to the quarterly service review | Tuomas Virta | 2026-10-31 | Still open |

## Lessons learned

1. **Documented diversity is not the same as physical diversity.** Architecture diagrams and descriptive documents can present a view of the network that does not match the ground reality. Procurement records that capture operational constraints must be reconciled with architecture documentation, and the higher-fidelity record (procurement) should take precedence when they disagree.

2. **Failover testing validates design assumptions.** A pre-armed test of the upstream circuit failover would have identified the shared-duct dependency before a contractor's digger exposed it. Failover tests should be a standard part of the quarterly service review for all customers with redundant circuits.

3. **Procurement notes must be acted on.** Identifying a risk and recording it in a procurement file is not sufficient. Identified risks must be escalated to a remediation owner with a due date and tracked to closure.

title: IT Asset Inventory Policy
body:
# IT Asset Inventory Policy

## 1. Purpose

This policy establishes the requirements for maintaining a complete and accurate inventory of all IT assets managed by Norvane Managed IT Services Oy. The asset register forms the single source of truth for asset ownership, lifecycle tracking, patch group assignment, and compliance reporting. It supports audit readiness under customer contracts and enables the procurement team to plan replacements before end-of-life dates are reached.

## 2. Scope

This policy applies to every managed device in the Norvane asset database — at a Norvane data centre, a customer site, or in transit. "Managed device" covers network equipment, servers, storage appliances, hypervisor hosts, VPN concentrators, and any hardware Norvane provisions, maintains, or monitors. End-user desktops and laptops are governed separately by the Service Desk.

## 3. What is recorded

Every managed device is entered into the inventory at the point of commissioning. The record is created from the deployment checklist that accompanies the change request (DOC-024) before the device is powered on or connected to the production network. Devices are removed from the inventory at decommissioning; they are not retained in an "active" table simply because the paperwork has not yet been processed. If a device is temporarily pulled from service for repair or firmware testing, it remains in the register with its criticality and patch group unchanged.

## 4. Record fields

The following fields are mandatory for every asset record in the inventory database (assets.csv and the corresponding BigQuery table):

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `asset_id` | Unique inventory identifier assigned at commissioning (format: `ASSET-YYYY-NNNN`). |
| `customer_id` | Customer contract code; use `NORVANE` for Norvane's own infrastructure. |
| `site` | Site identifier matching the canonical site names in DOC-011 (e.g. `dc1`, `dc2`, `aurora-hq`). |
| `hostname` | Device hostname following the naming convention in DOC-012 (e.g. `core-sw-01`). |
| `device_type` | Category of the device: switch, router, firewall, server, storage, hypervisor, or other. |
| `vendor_model` | Vendor name and model string (e.g. `Cisco Catalyst 9500-48Y4C`). |
| `mgmt_ip` | Management-plane IP address as documented in DOC-011. |
| `firmware_version` | Current running firmware or OS version (e.g. `IOS-XE 17.9.4a`). |
| `end_of_life_date` | Vendor-published end-of-life or end-of-sale date. |
| `criticality` | Classification of `critical`, `high`, `medium`, or `low`. |
| `patch_group` | Automated patch group derived from the criticality value (see §5). |

## 5. Ownership and reconciliation

The Service Delivery Manager owns the inventory for customer-provided devices; the Head of Infrastructure owns Norvane-owned infrastructure. Reconciliation against Zabbix (DOC-021) and the DHCP reservations database occurs quarterly. The diff report flags devices in monitoring but absent from the register — or vice versa — triggering an investigation ticket within two business days. The report is filed in the SharePoint asset management library.

## 6. End-of-life management

Devices approaching end of life are identified through the `end_of_life_date` field. A replacement plan must be initiated twelve months before the vendor's end-of-sale date. The plan includes budget allocation, procurement lead-time assessment, and a migration window coordinated with the customer as a change request. Devices that have passed their end-of-life date without an approved replacement plan are flagged as `critical - at risk` and escalated to the Head of Infrastructure for resolution within thirty days.

## 7. Disposal

Disposal of a physical asset requires certified data wiping using a tool approved by the Security Lead under DOC-025. Wiping is verified and a certificate of destruction or data sanitisation is generated. The asset record is updated to reflect the disposal date, the method of wiping, and the certificate reference. The disposal record — including the certificate — is retained for six years after the date of disposal and is stored in the document management system alongside the original change ticket. Physical assets are removed from the customer site only after written confirmation from the customer's site representative where the device was located.

## 8. Exceptions

Any deviation from this policy — including failure to record a device or incorrect criticality — must be documented with justification and approved by the asset's designated owner. Exceptions are reviewed at each quarterly reconciliation. Persistent non-compliance is escalated to the Service Delivery Manager.

title: Privileged Access Management Policy
body:
# Privileged Access Management Policy

## 1. Purpose

This policy governs all privileged access to the Norvane infrastructure. It ensures that administrative rights are assigned on a need-to-have basis, that every privileged action is attributable to a named individual, and that privileged sessions are recorded and auditable.

## 2. Scope

This policy applies to every individual requiring privileged access to systems within the Norvane managed environment or customer environments. It covers network devices (switches, routers, firewalls), hypervisor platforms (VMware vSphere), backup appliances (Dell PowerProtect DP4400), domain controllers, and the bastion host. It applies to Norvane employees, contractors, and third-party personnel granted access.

## 3. Principles

Privileged access is governed by the following principles:

- No shared accounts. Every administrator is assigned a named personal account used exclusively by that individual.
- No standing privilege where just-in-time (JIT) elevation is available. Where the platform supports JIT, the default state is privileged-off; elevation requires an approval step.
- Credentials are never stored in documents, spreadsheets, email, or chat applications. All secrets — passwords, API tokens, and keys — are stored exclusively in the vault.
- Access is granted by role and customer contract, never by individual request alone.

## 4. Accounts

Four account categories exist under this policy:

**Personal named accounts.** Every administrator receives a personal account on each platform. On network devices, authentication uses TACACS+. The server enforces per-user credentials and logs all login attempts.

**Break-glass accounts.** Exactly one local break-glass account exists per device family. The credential is held in the vault and is reserved for when the primary authentication system is unavailable. Activation raises an immediate alert to the security team.

**Service accounts.** Service accounts support automated processes, backup jobs, and monitoring integrations. Every service account is inventoried and documented in the vault with its purpose, owner, and last rotation date. Credentials are rotated at least annually as part of the vault rotation cycle.

**Customer break-glass accounts.** For customer sites requiring a break-glass procedure, Norvane maintains one account per device family accessible only via vault checkout. The customer is informed at the time of checkout.

## 5. Access path

All privileged administrative access must be performed through the bastion host. The bastion is the only system permitted for direct SSH, HTTPS, or console access to production devices. Direct management-plane access from user networks and the client VPN is prohibited (see DOC-015). This applies to all administrators, including senior staff.

## 6. Session controls

All privileged sessions are subject to the following controls:

- Multi-factor authentication required for every login to the bastion and any privileged platform.
- Sessions are recorded (terminal audio and command log), retained for twelve months.
- A deny-list of sensitive commands (e.g. firewall rule deletion, VLAN reconfiguration) requires a second approver in the bastion host.
- Idle sessions are terminated after sixty minutes.
- Access is logged to the central syslog collector and forwarded to the SIEM for real-time alerting.

## 7. Emergency access

Emergency access is used when a production-impacting incident requires immediate privileged action:

1. The administrator checks out the break-glass credential from the vault, recording the reason in the audit field.
2. The vault sends automatic notification to the Security Lead.
3. The administrator performs the remediation; all actions are recorded in the vault session log.
4. Within five business days, the Security Lead and Head of Infrastructure conduct a retrospective review to assess whether the emergency was justified.
5. A post-incident report is filed as a change record (CHG-YYYY-NNNN) or a postmortem.

## 8. Recertification

Privileged access is recertified quarterly by the Head of Infrastructure, who reviews each active account and confirms access is still required. Unrecertified accounts are revoked automatically within twenty-four hours of the deadline.

## 9. Records

Session recordings: twelve months. Break-glass checkout logs: indefinitely. Recertification reports: seven years. Emergency access reviews: six years. Service account inventory: updated at every rotation.

title: New Starter IT Onboarding Checklist
body:
# New Starter IT Onboarding Checklist

## 1. Purpose

This checklist ensures new Norvane employees and contractors receive the IT access, equipment, and training required for their role before they begin. The Service Desk executes each item. The hiring manager ensures the request is raised in time and role-specific items are communicated.

## 2. Before day one

The hiring manager raises the onboarding request at least five business days before the start date. It must include the employee's full legal name, job title, department, start date, line manager, and a role description.

- [ ] Confirm the request was raised at least five business days before the start date. Short-notice requests are flagged to the hiring manager for deferral.
- [ ] Verify identity against the HR record. Accounts are created from the HR record, not from the email address.
- [ ] Create the user identity in Active Directory, created in a disabled state to be enabled on first morning.
- [ ] Determine role-specific additions from Section 5. Mark N/A with a reason if none apply.
- [ ] Prepare a laptop with the standard image (DOC-025). Must be encrypted before handover.
- [ ] Reserve a desk and equipment (monitor, docking station, headset) for the workspace.

## 3. Day one

The Service Desk executes these items on the first morning before any team meeting.

- [ ] Enable the Active Directory account. Confirm login by having the new starter change their temporary password.
- [ ] Enrol in MFA using the corporate authenticator. Confirm MFA is active and a backup code recorded.
- [ ] Issue the laptop. Verify full-disk encryption is active and the device is enrolled in endpoint management.
- [ ] Connect to corporate Wi-Fi by distributing the Wi-Fi profile (802.1X with PEAP-MSCHAPv2).
- [ ] Install and configure the VPN client per DOC-015. Confirm VPN connection with the correct network access profile.
- [ ] Create and configure the mailbox. Verify email send/receive and global address list visibility.
- [ ] Provision a ticket system account. Confirm login and test ticket creation.
- [ ] Provide DOC-025 and DOC-041 for reading.
- [ ] Record acknowledgement of DOC-025 and DOC-041 in the onboarding ticket, including timestamp and identity.

## 4. First week

The following items must be completed within the new starter's first seven calendar days.

- [ ] Enrol the new starter in the on-call rota shadow for their team. The shadow rotation runs for two weeks; the new starter is not paged during this period.
- [ ] Assign the security awareness training module. Confirm completion within the first five business days.
- [ ] Verify that the new starter's access entitlements match their role. Compare the assigned groups and permissions against the role matrix maintained by the Service Desk Team Lead.
- [ ] Confirm that the new starter has received and acknowledged the Norvane acceptable-use policy.

## 5. Role-specific additions

Items in this section apply only to certain roles, specified by the hiring manager at request time.

- [ ] **Administrators**: Request bastion host access from the Security Lead per DOC-041. Approval required before creation. Confirm MFA enrolment on the bastion.
- [ ] **Network engineers**: Provision read-only device access for thirty days. Write access is added after thirty days with line manager confirmation.
- [ ] **Customer-facing roles**: Assign customer portal login for assigned accounts. Verify access against the customer contract tier.

## 6. First 30 days

- [ ] Conduct an access review with the line manager. Confirm entitlements are appropriate and no excess access was granted.
- [ ] Confirm no unexplained accounts or permissions in any system.
- [ ] Verify equipment is functioning correctly (laptop, VPN, Wi-Fi, mailbox).
- [ ] Complete and close the onboarding ticket only after all items are ticked.

## 7. Records and audit

Onboarding tickets are retained for six years after the new starter's end date (or contract end) in the ITSM system. Supporting records — MFA enrolment, equipment issue logs, training certificates, and policy receipts — are also retained for six years. The Service Desk Team Lead reviews a random sample of closed tickets each quarter.
